identity.title: Stable Anthocyanin Accumulation in Vegetable Crops: Multilayer Molecular Regulation, Edible-Tissue Constraints and Biotechnological Improvement.

content.abstract: Anthocyanins are multifunctional flavonoid pigments that contribute to red, purple, and blue coloration, oxidative stress protection, nutritional quality, and market value in vegetable crops. However, their accumulation in edible tissues is often low, unstable, tissue-specific, and restricted to particular developmental stages, limiting their use in crop improvement and natural colorant production. This suggests that anthocyanin enrichment is not solely controlled by biosynthesis, but rather by the coordinated regulation of precursor flux, MYB-bHLH-WD40-mediated transcription, post-transcriptional and chromatin-based control, pigment modification, transport, sequestration, and degradation. Recent transcriptomic, metabolomic, and epigenomic studies have improved our understanding of how environmental signals, including light, temperature, nutrient status, and phytohormones, interact with these regulatory layers to shape anthocyanin accumulation and retention in vegetable crops. Biotechnological approaches, including CRISPR/Cas9, CRISPRa, metabolic engineering, and multi-omics-guided target discovery, provide new opportunities to improve pigment stability by targeting key biosynthetic and regulatory genes. This review synthesizes recent progress in vegetable crops, especially Solanaceae and Brassicaceae, with emphasis on the molecular constraints that limit stable pigmentation in edible tissues. We highlight that future improvement should move beyond darker phenotypes and focus on the coordinated regulation of synthesis, stabilization, vacuolar retention, and degradation control to develop anthocyanin-enriched vegetables with improved nutritional quality, climate resilience, and market value.
